text:
I have been thinking this week about what happens one line after a success metric.

A stove is distributed. A loan is approved. A household is connected to electricity.

All three can be genuine progress. But my team’s research this week kept returning to the same question: what has to happen next for that progress to last?

Our clean-cooking paper looked at Africa’s rapid move towards LPG. More than 70% of clean-cooking access now comes from it. That has real health and practical benefits, but it also concentrates households around a fuel exposed to global supply shocks and price swings. Financially, resilience matters because adoption that collapses after a shock wastes capital. Ethically, a transition is not much of a transition if families are pushed back towards smoke when supply fails.

https://stonecomms.com/research/blue-flame-chokepoint-africa-clean-cooking-resilience

Our second paper looked at finance for women-owned businesses. IFC’s new guarantee programme can unlock much more local lending than the public capital behind it. But guarantees solve the lender’s risk problem; they do not automatically make a business visible, documented, appropriately served or connected to a market. The financial question is how to turn risk-sharing into viable lending. The ethical question is whether exclusion simply moves elsewhere in the system.

https://stonecomms.com/research/missing-balance-sheet-womens-finance-africa

The third paper asks what happens after an electricity connection. Mission 300 has already connected more than 50 million people. The next challenge is productive demand: pumps, cold rooms, clinics, workshops and charging hubs that make power useful and improve the economics of the energy asset.

That matters financially because better utilisation can strengthen revenues. It matters socially because electricity should expand what people and communities can actually do, not merely improve a connection count.

https://stonecomms.com/research/kilowatt-after-connection-mission-300-productive-use

The common thread is simple. Infrastructure is rarely finished when the visible thing arrives. The harder work is making systems keep working, reach the right people and create value over time.

Coming up next, my team is looking at whether African trade corridors are operationally integrated as well as physically connected; whether cold-chain projects are designed around useful service rather than equipment; and whether nature-based protection can be managed with the same discipline as conventional infrastructure.
